document.title: Deputy Secretary Armitage's Meeting with General Mahmud: Actions and Support Expected of Pakistan in Fight Against Terrorism (State 159711)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
document.note: [Secret] Armitage again meets ISI Chief Mahmoud Ahmed and lists specific requests for Musharraf's approval: stop al-Qaida operatives at the border, intercept arms shipments, end logistical support for bin Laden, grant overflight and territorial access, share intelligence, cut off fuel and recruits to the Taliban, and break relations with the Taliban if evidence implicates bin Laden. Less redacted than the 2010 version.

events.description: Armitage met ISI DG Mahmud Ahmed and delivered a nonpaper of US demands on Pakistan after 9/11.
Mahmud met JCS Deputy General Abizaid at the Pentagon earlier that morning.
Armitage gave an earlier message to Mahmud (REF A).
Terrorist attacks of September 11 referenced as the trigger for demands.
Terrorist attacks on the US referred to as 'Tuesday's attacks' and 'September 11'.
Armitage gave Mahmud an earlier message the previous day (REF A).
Armitage met Mahmud and gave a nonpaper listing US requests of Pakistan: border interdiction, overflight, access, intelligence, cut off Taliban supplies, possible break with Taliban.
Mahmud stated Pakistan stood with the US and promised to pass the message to his government.
State Department instructs Ambassador Chamberlin to double-track the nonpaper with Musharraf.

key_claims: The US demanded Pakistan stop al-Qa'ida operatives at the border, intercept arms and end logistical support for bin Ladin.
The US demanded blanket overflight, landing rights and territorial access, including naval ports and airbases.
Pakistan was asked to cut off fuel, supplies and volunteers going to the Taliban in Afghanistan.
If bin Ladin was implicated and Taliban kept harboring him, Pakistan was to break relations with the Taliban and end support.
ISI chief Mahmud pledged Pakistan stood with the US and asked about military consultative mechanisms.
